title: A court of many faiths
hookLine: a Muslim foreign minister, Hindu and Dogra ministers, and European officers served at his court

lines: A MUSLIM SCHOLAR SPEAKS FOR LAHORE.
cards: A foreign visitor at the Lahore court is shown in by a man in a Muslim scholar's dress, who speaks for the kingdom.

Across the hall stand Hindu officials who keep the accounts, Dogra brothers from the hills who manage the Maharaja's household, Sikh generals with their turbans and swords, and a few officers in European coats who drill the army.
All of them answer to one man.

teach.b: The man who spoke for the kingdom was Fakir Azizuddin: a Muslim, a physician and a scholar, the Maharaja's trusted adviser and envoy.
When the British or the Afghans needed to hear from Lahore, he was often the one they heard, and histories remember his tact and his learning.
The Dogra brothers, Gulab Singh and Dhian Singh among them, rose high at court, and Dhian Singh became chief minister.
Hindu officials ran the treasury and the revenue, and Hindu commanders, like the general who took Kashmir, led armies.
You've already met the European officers who trained the army; some had served Napoleon, histories say, and came to Lahore and stayed. What held it together?

teach.h: A KHALSA STATE, MANY FAITHS IN IT.
teach.b: This was the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name, with coins struck in the Gurus' names, yet the people running it came from many faiths. Sikh tradition points back to the Gurus for the reason.
In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the Guru says he is neither Hindu nor Muslim: his body and breath belong to the One whom Hindus call Ram and Muslims call Allah.
It wasn't perfect, and the ministers' rivalries will matter later in this story. But the Maharaja chose people for what they could do, and let them keep their own way of praying.

how: Sikhs often point to Maharaja Ranjit Singh's court, with its Muslim, Hindu, Dogra, Sikh and European officials, as an example of the Gurus' teaching of one Lord whom Hindus and Muslims each name in their own way.

o: a Muslim scholar who served as the Maharaja's envoy
a Dogra minister who ran the Maharaja's household
a Sufi saint whose shrine stood beside Lahore Fort

games.q: who served the court — tap the pairs.

s: only Sikhs held high office at the Lahore court
a Muslim envoy, Dogra and Hindu ministers and European officers served too.
in a hymn, Guru Arjan says he is neither Hindu nor Muslim
his body and breath belong to the One that Hindus call Ram and Muslims call Allah.
it wasn't perfect, and the ministers' rivalries matter later in the story.

games.q: you rule a kingdom in the Khalsa's name. the best envoy you can find is a Muslim scholar. what do you do?
o: pass him over for a Sikh.
make him your trusted adviser and envoy.
games.why: Fakir Azizuddin served the Maharaja as adviser and envoy and kept his own faith.

practice: Bring to mind the people in your daily life who differ from you in faith, background, age or way of doing things, and picture them one by one.
For each, name one thing they do well, something you'd want on your team, and let the list grow. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Fakir Azizuddin, the Muslim physician and envoy who spoke for Lahore, serving a court of many faiths: Dogra and Hindu ministers, Sikh generals and European officers, all serving one Khalsa kingdom.

orig.note: darbar, the court; Sikhs also use it for the Guru's court, as in Darbar Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: many faiths, one court. A kingdom in the Khalsa's name had room for all of them. See you tomorrow.
